name: Google Cloud Run
summary: Give Google a container that listens on a port; it runs as many copies as traffic needs, down to zero.
intro: Cloud Run runs any container image that serves HTTP. Each deploy creates a revision, and Cloud Run starts instances of it as requests arrive. Unlike Lambda, one instance handles many requests at once: up to 80 per vCPU by default when deployed from the CLI, configurable up to 1,000. When traffic stops, idle instances are kept for up to 15 minutes and then the service scales to zero. Instances go up to 8 vCPU and 32 GiB, a request can run for up to 60 minutes, and GPUs are available for inference.

Besides request-driven services, Cloud Run has jobs, which run a container to completion (as many parallel tasks as you ask for, each for up to 7 days) and worker pools for always-on background consumers. You can deploy from source in Go, Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, Ruby or PHP and Cloud Run builds the image for you. Billing is either request-based (no charge while an instance isn’t handling a request) or instance-based (pay for the instance’s whole lifetime, no per-request fee).
strengths: Plain containers: any language or binary, and the same image runs locally or on Kubernetes
Scales to zero, so a quiet service costs nothing on request-based billing
Concurrency per instance means fewer cold starts and better use of memory than one-request-per-instance platforms
Services, batch jobs and background workers on one platform with the same deploy model
limits: Cold starts after scaling to zero; set minimum instances to keep some warm, which you pay for
Instances top out at 8 vCPU and 32 GiB, and files written to local disk use up the instance’s memory
If all instances are busy, requests wait briefly and then fail with HTTP 429
Google Cloud only; the API and IAM model don’t carry over to other clouds

story: Google had offered serverless hosting since App Engine’s preview in April 2008, but on its terms: at first only Python, code written exclusively in Python, no writing to the filesystem, and responses due within a few seconds. Containers later became the standard way to package any app, yet running them meant operating a Kubernetes cluster. Google’s launch post summed up the dilemma: developers had to choose “between the ease and velocity that comes with serverless or the flexibility and portability that comes with containers”.

Google announced Cloud Run on April 9, 2019, in a post by Eyal Manor and Oren Teich. You hand it a stateless container that serves HTTP, and it scales the container up within seconds and down to zero. Google said it was based on Knative, an open-source API for serverless workloads on Kubernetes (first commit January 2018), so the same service could also run on a GKE cluster or anyone’s Kubernetes. Google later clarified that fully managed Cloud Run doesn’t use Knative itself but stays compatible with the Knative API. Cloud Run became generally available on November 14, 2019, billed to the nearest 100 milliseconds, alongside Cloud Run for Anthos (since renamed Knative serving) for GKE clusters in Google Cloud or on premises.
Since then it has grown from a web-request runner into a general compute platform: 60-minute requests in 2021, batch jobs in 2023, GPUs in 2025 and always-on worker pools in 2026.

choices.choice: Any container that listens on a port
choices.why: Earlier serverless platforms limited your language, libraries and filesystem. Accepting a plain container image removed those limits and meant the same image could run on a laptop or a cluster.

choices.choice: Compatible with the open Knative API
choices.why: Google’s pitch answered the fear of lock-in: a Knative service definition could move between fully managed Cloud Run, GKE and other Kubernetes clusters, even though the managed service doesn’t run Knative itself.
Unlike one-request-per-instance functions, a Cloud Run instance serves up to 80 requests per vCPU by default, so fewer instances (and fewer cold starts) handle the same traffic.

choices.choice: A gVisor sandbox first, a microVM later
choices.why: gVisor intercepts system calls in user space, which starts fast but can’t emulate every Linux feature. A second-generation microVM environment, generally available in 2022, gave full Linux compatibility for apps that needed it.

timeline.text: App Engine preview: Google’s first managed platform for running apps
Cloud Run announced in April; generally available on November 14
60-minute request timeouts and up to 1,000 concurrent requests per instance
Second-generation microVM execution environment reaches general availability
Cloud Run jobs for run-to-completion work become generally available
GPUs generally available in April for inference workloads
Worker pools for always-on background work reach general availability
